name: Cryptic crossword No 22,190
preamble: Solutions to the asterisked clues are all characters with a reason to celebrate today.

clue.text: Vehicle used to carry people away

definitions.note: a description of a thing, standing for the noun: something used for this

blocks.note: first meaning: a large lorry for moving cars or heavy loads
second meaning: whatever sends people into raptures, or once shipped convicts overseas

explanation.surface: A coach or minibus laid on to ferry a crowd off somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one description of a bus; the second half is really to transport in its emotional sense, to carry away with delight.
explanation.definitionFit: A large lorry built for moving cargo or cars is named for that job, and literally the word means one that enraptures or deports.

indicators.note: something awkward is clumsy and out of place, so these letters must be put into a new order

blocks.note: a small common songbird
abbreviation for the United States
with in the sense of plus
standard abbreviation for right
the six letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird-watching relative from America who is socially clumsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle celebrates Shakespeare's birthday, 23 April; TITUS ANDRONICUS is the general who gives his name to the early revenge tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the Roman general at the heart of Shakespeare's bloodiest tragedy, so a character with a reason to celebrate the playwright's birthday.

clue.text: A man, perhaps, in the passage

blocks.note: taken as written
Man, capitalised in the reading, is the Isle of Man; perhaps marks it as one example of an island

explanation.surface: Some fellow standing about in a corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter of Man is hidden by the sentence; the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A walkway between rows of seats in a church, theatre or aircraft is a narrow passage.

blocks.note: a secret agent; the possessive just ties him to the next word
to be in a hole is to be in a fix or predicament

explanation.surface: A secret agent's predicament made him squint, or was merely a quick glance.
explanation.walkthrough: A squint is also an oblique opening cut through a church wall to give a view of the altar.
explanation.definitionFit: A squint in architecture is a small peeping opening, the same thing as a little hole for looking through a door.

blocks.note: surface reading: a venue where delegates meet for a conference
setter's reading: Conference is a popular variety of pear, so its centre is where the fruit trees grow

explanation.walkthrough: Conference is the commonest pear grown in Britain; the question mark warns that the venue is not a meeting hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot of fruit trees is where Conference pears are grown and harvested, making it their home base.

clue.text: Bear has role to play in modern art show

indicators.note: letters set to play are free to move about and rearrange themselves
one group of letters goes inside another

blocks.note: first half of the Tate, home of the Tate Modern gallery in London
the four letters rearranged
second half of the same gallery name

explanation.surface: An actor in a bear costume performs in an exhibition of contemporary art.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's national gallery group, Tate Modern its contemporary art venue; the jumbled four letters sit after its first T.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something unpleasant is to put up with it or endure it without complaint.

indicators.note: ruin wrecks the words that follow, so their letters are rebuilt in a different order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of these three words go into the mix

explanation.surface: A warning that downstream there will be either destruction or a flood.
explanation.walkthrough: ROBIN GOODFELLOW is Puck's other name in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a mischievous sprite who might well cause such havoc.
explanation.definitionFit: Puck, the fairy servant of Oberon, is called by this name in Shakespeare's comedy, so he celebrates the writer's birthday.

clue.text: Sloth! One needs help to recover

indicators.note: read as re-cover, going back over the word, so it is taken from its end

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
a plain synonym, read backwards here

explanation.surface: A lazy person admits they need assistance to get well again.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the medieval spiritual sloth counted among the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare word names listless apathy, the deadly sin of sloth as the medieval Church described it.

blocks.note: un is the French for a
to pack a gap or hole is to stuff or plug it

explanation.surface: Someone unwraps a packet bought in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Pack is a verb here, as in packing a wound, not a bundle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling the stopper out of a drain or blocked pipe frees and clears the way, so it opens it up.

indicators.note: wild letters are untamed and running loose, so they settle in a new order
an empty word has had its inside cleared out, leaving just its two ends
one group of letters is placed inside another

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word for a town
the five letters reshuffled
the final letter of the word for a town

explanation.surface: A savage animal loose in a deserted town.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir William CATESBY is Richard III's loyal henchman in Shakespeare's history play.
explanation.definitionFit: He is a supporting figure in Richard III, one of the characters marking the playwright's birthday, as the preamble says.

indicators.note: one group of letters sits inside another, as a prisoner sits in a cell

blocks.note: first letter of can, slang for jail
taken as written
the usual short form of Liberal
rest of can, American slang for jail

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician finds himself locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: CALIBAN is the savage, enslaved creature of The Tempest, himself confined by Prospero, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero's monstrous servant on the island in The Tempest is one of the characters celebrating Shakespeare's birthday.

indicators.note: the letters are found in the middle of the run of words that follows

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word to the start of the third

explanation.surface: Something at the heart of the Marquis de Sade's devilish performance.
explanation.walkthrough: DESDEMONA is Othello's wife, smothered by her jealous husband; the Marquis de Sade was the notorious French writer of cruelty.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's innocent wife is one of Shakespeare's best-known heroines, so she belongs among the characters celebrating his birthday.

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the next word is altered into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the five letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A patient urges a physician to study up on the kidneys.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor looks like the person addressed, and the medical setting makes that natural; it is the verb that signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from the Latin for kidney, so it describes anything relating to those organs.

clue.text: A northern pair of opposing players

blocks.note: taken as written
abbreviation for north
in bridge, North and East sit on opposite sides, so they are opponents

explanation.surface: Two rival sportsmen from the north of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady ANNE is wooed by Richard over her father-in-law's coffin in Richard III; bridge players are named by compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Anne, widow who marries Richard of Gloucester, is a character in Richard III and so a celebrant of Shakespeare's birthday.

indicators.note: treating something means processing it, working it into a changed form

blocks.note: all ten letters, the possessive s included

explanation.surface: A vet or doctor attends to a dragon's skin complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Rash looks like the noun, a skin eruption needing treatment; it is the adjective meaning reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash person acts impetuously without thinking, just as a wilful, impetuous one does.

clue.text: The policy of being a part not apart

definitions.text: The policy of being a part not apart

blocks.note: surface reading: a play on two spellings, being included rather than separate
setter's reading: a political doctrine favouring staying joined, as Northern Ireland with Britain

explanation.walkthrough: In British and Irish politics the term names the cause of keeping Northern Ireland, or Scotland, inside the United Kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine favours remaining joined in a single federation rather than separating, exactly being one part of a whole.

clue.text: Sources, first, of small and pretty fairy rings

indicators.note: asks for the opening letter of each of the next words named

blocks.note: opening letter
opening letter
the circles of dark grass said to be made by dancing fairies; Prospero calls them green sour ringlets

explanation.surface: An enquiry into the origins of small, pretty rings in the grass said to be made by fairies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tempest's ringlets are fairy rings, a fitting Shakespearean touch in this puzzle; the answer means little springs.
explanation.definitionFit: Small springs are points where water rises from the ground, the sources of streams.

indicators.note: one group of letters goes inside another
a problem is something to be worked out, so these letters must be sorted into a new order

blocks.note: first part of the rearranged pair of words
56 written in Roman numerals: fifty, five, one
last letter of the rearranged pair

explanation.surface: A schoolboy finds fifty-six in his Latin homework a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: SILVIA is the Duke's daughter loved by Valentine in The Two Gentlemen of Verona, wooed with the song Who is Silvia?
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of The Two Gentlemen of Verona, praised in a famous song, is one of the playwright's characters marking his birthday.

blocks.note: first meaning: failed someone's hopes, as a verb in the past tense
second meaning: lowered, as a rope or a basket from a window

explanation.surface: Someone is upset at being left out of the team.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads dropped as being axed from a side; the second sense is simply lowered.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both failed someone who relied on you and lowered something gradually, as on a rope.

blocks.note: first meaning: by means of, because of
second meaning: of a train, running non-stop from end to end

explanation.surface: A request to convey one's gratitude.
explanation.walkthrough: Express looks like a verb, to voice thanks, but it is the adjective used of a fast train.
explanation.definitionFit: As a preposition the word means owing to, and of a train or ticket it means going direct without stopping.

blocks.note: the first-person pronoun
a den is a small private room for reading or working

explanation.surface: Who was the very first to take up a subject at university?
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander IDEN is the Kentish gentleman who kills the rebel Jack Cade in Henry VI Part 2.
explanation.definitionFit: This minor squire from Henry VI Part 2 is one of the playwright's characters, so he joins the birthday celebrations.

indicators.note: something thrown is tossed about, so the word's letters land in a different order

blocks.note: the five letters reshuffled
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A rock is hurled at a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: NESTOR is the aged, long-winded Greek counsellor in Troilus and Cressida.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Greek general advising the besiegers of Troy appears in Troilus and Cressida, making him a Shakespearean character.

clue.text: Language used for little entrance in Scotland

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for little
Scots word for the reveal or side of a doorway or window opening

explanation.surface: A word Scots use for a small doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish ingo is the side wall of a door or window recess; the surface suggests looking up dialect, which fits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially this word means a language or dialect, especially jargon or a foreign tongue that is hard to follow.

blocks.note: surface reading: needles lacking sharp tips are useless
setter's reading: sewing needles are of no use unless someone or something puts cotton through the eye

explanation.walkthrough: Pointless seems to mean blunt; it means purposeless, since an unloaded needle cannot sew.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people or small gadgets that pass cotton through the eye of a sewing needle so it can be used.

indicators.note: a section is a cut piece of a longer thing, here of the word before
in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: five letters lying inside this word

explanation.surface: An aircraft touches down with part of its wheels retracted.
explanation.walkthrough: Landed looks like a plane arriving; it is the adjective meaning owning land, as in landed gentry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone owning many acres holds estates, as a member of the landed gentry does.

indicators.note: one word is placed so that it surrounds another

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
from the French à, with, as in à la or café au lait
first letter of CO, the abbreviation for company
taken as written
second letter of the same abbreviation

explanation.surface: A person who never travels without friends in attendance.
explanation.walkthrough: IACHIMO is the Italian schemer of Cymbeline who hides in a trunk in Imogen's bedroom. With giving A is weak; the setter may intend One as I and A together.
explanation.definitionFit: The villainous Italian who wagers on Imogen's chastity in Cymbeline is one of Shakespeare's characters celebrating his birthday.

clue.text: I'll tour around to find this artist

indicators.note: the letters are turned about and moved round into a new order

blocks.note: all seven letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A traveller plans a round trip to track down a favourite painter's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Maurice UTRILLO was the French painter of Montmartre street scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a French painter famed for views of Paris streets, so he is the painter the clue points to.

blocks.note: the name that goes with both: Simple Simon of the nursery rhyme and Simon Pure, the genuine article
to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: A basic description of an uncomplicated or pedigree dog.
explanation.walkthrough: SIMON SHADOW is a scrawny recruit pressed by Falstaff in Henry IV Part 2. Simon Pure, from an 18th-century comedy, means the real thing.
explanation.definitionFit: This feeble conscript mustered by Falstaff in Henry IV Part 2 is a minor Shakespearean character with reason to celebrate.
